teaching.task: # HMS Year 11 V13 (Health for individuals and communities): young people as advocates. How have young people changed the conditions that shape health, and what makes advocacy work rather than just raise awareness? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: That's advocacy: speaking or acting to change the conditions, decisions or policies that affect health, your own or other people's. Every personal skill so far works on what a person does. Advocacy works on what they're doing it within, and it's how young people push for the regulation, services and environments you met earlier. So it isn't health education, which teaches someone something. It isn't awareness-raising, which makes an issue visible but asks nobody to act. And it isn't personal behaviour change, which aims at column one. It also runs two ways. Self-advocacy is acting for your own health, like asking a doctor for a referral. Advocacy for others acts for people who can't easily act for themselves. Every piece of advocacy needs two things: an ask, the one specific thing you want done, and an audience, the decision-maker who can grant it. Raise awareness of youth mental health fails both. Ask the council to run the last bus past the youth health centre until seven pm, not five, passes both, and it's small enough to win. A specific ask aimed at the body that can say yes beats a big campaign aimed at nobody. To examine a campaign, the syllabus says use various sources, and various means different kinds, not three news articles. Each kind fails in its own way. News covers the launch, and rarely says whether anything changed a year later. Campaign material states the ask, but reports its own success. Government reports are detailed, but slow. And social media shows reach, but engagement isn't impact. So ask four questions of every source. Who made it, and what did they want? When, and has anything happened since? Is it claiming something happened, or that something worked? And what would disagree with it?

scenes.teachingReason: That's advocacy: speaking or acting to change the conditions, decisions or policies that affect health, your own or other people's. Every personal skill so far works on what a person does. Advocacy works on what they're doing it within, and it's how young people push for the regulation, services and environments you met earlier. So it isn't health education, which teaches someone something. It isn't awareness-raising, which makes an issue visible but asks nobody to act. And it isn't personal behaviour change, which aims at column one. It also runs two ways. Self-advocacy is acting for your own health, like asking a doctor for a referral. Advocacy for others acts for people who can't easily act for themselves.

scenes.teachingReason: Finally, the syllabus asks about individuals within their communities, and within is the key word. Advocacy has a range of reach. Self-advocacy, then speaking up for one other person, then acting through a structure that already exists, like a student council, club or cultural organisation, then an organised campaign, and finally policy. A principal wants a short costed proposal. A formal inquiry wants a submission. The public wants one clear story.
